The Black Mambas

By: Graham Coetzer | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
They're called the Black Mambas - and they're the world's first all-female anti-poaching unit - we meet some of the women on the front lines of a desperate fight to save our wildlife.

Unique Selling Point:
The Black Mambas, named after the well known venomous snake, are 36 young African women who patrol 20 000 hectares of game reserve in the Greater Kruger National Park. Kruger is home to the largest population of Rhino in the world and has also been the vitim of the most poaching attacks. Unlike the gung-ho approach of many anti-poaching units, the Mamba's patrol unarmed, and are spearheading a uniquely South African, innovative approach to wildlife conservation.

The Mamba's are focussing their efforts on buy-in from local communities in the area's around Kruger - the same communities where poverty and hardship mean people are easily recruited by poaching syndicates. They also provide eye's and ears on the ground in the areas they patrol. They report, track and trace suspected poaching incursions, destroy bush-meat kitchens and poaching camps, as well as remove remove snares.

Summary:
Their efforts have paid off, they've been incredibly successful in their areas of operation. What's more, they've proven that women can play a valuable role in anti-poaching efforts, a traditionally male dominated field.

But who are the women behind the name? In our story we will get to know one or two of the Mamba's, and find out how their own personal struggles have shaped their destinies and lead them into a life on the frontlines of the fight against the international illicit wildlife trade. We'll meet women like Seargeant Leita Nkabela, who grew up in a nearby village. Her family struggled to just put food on the table, and the Kruger Park was seen as a place for the rich, a place they could not visit. But when her brother became a game ranger, Leita's own perceptions on wildlife conservation started to shift. Tragically, her brother was killed in a skirmish with poachers... So why did she decide to get involved?



Further information:
The Black Mambas have had some media exposure, most of it internationally. They are stoked to have Carte Blanche do the story, and have offered us all access.



Extra Budget Items:
Accomodation for presenter, producer and crew near the Mamba's headquarters.

I'm happy to use my own vehicle, and will claim for fuel purchased.

Script:


Black Mambas
First Draft Script
24 June 2024

Intro

Voice
A place where two worlds collide: one, the splendour of the South African bush...

The other, an illicit and ruthless criminal enterprise.

In the middle, an animal whose numbers have been in sharp decline, the centrepiece of global conservation efforts.
ACT1

Upsound Mambas on parade.

Voice
An early morning parade about 30 kilometres outside the town of Hoedspruit in the low veld.

Upsound Mambas on parade

Voice
To an outsider it might seem like another of the country’s many para-military security units… but this group is different.

Upsound Mambas on Parade.
Stand at ease!

Link Govan
When you think anti-poaching, you think guys in the bush with big guns. But sometimes, you need a woman’s touch to get the job done.

Voice
Named after the venomous snake whose bite is known as the ‘kiss of death’, the Black Mambas are the world’s first all female anti-poaching unit.

Upsound Nkateko Mzimba
So many people they are undermining us. They say how can you catch a poacher, how can you defend yourself on poachers, and I say: It’s good to listen, to observe, and then you can be safe in the bush.

Voice
Few offices in the world could offer you a view like this one. For Nkateko Mzimba, it’s the kind of scene that inspired her passion for conservation.

Upsound Nkateko
It’s different to stay in the city, and in the bush. For me when I’m in the bush, I love the bush more than anything. Why? Because those animals they need us to protect them.

Voice
It’s a peaceful scene. We examine fresh spoor and watch the herd make their near silent trek through the undergrowth.

It’s hard to imagine anything bad happening here.

But tonight’s full moon is a somber omen of what lies in store for the Mambas.

Link Govan
Okay - we’ve arrived at Olifant’s West, and it’s a nature reserve that’s part of the greater Kruger. Which means there are no fences between this place and the Kruger Park. And I’m about to join the Black Mambas on night patrol.

Voice
This is part of about 20 000 hectares of bush that the Mamba’s look after.

It’s also the world’s hardest hit rhino poaching area. According to some studies the Kruger park has seen a 60% decline in its rhino population since 2013.

The poaching is fuelled by organised crime syndicates who smuggle rhino horn to the international black market.

It’s a lucrative and violent world.

Link Govan
There’s a full moon, or as some people like to call it, the poaching moon. It means the poachers can see it at night.

Voice
We’ve started our patrol with a perimeter fence inspection.

Dusk soon gives way to full darkness.

Upsound Debra Mukansi
Govan: Am I the only one that’s nervous?

Debra: Ja! (Laughter)

Govan: Hau, Debra.

Voice
Surprisingly, unlike similar units, the Black Mambas don’t carry guns.

Drive by shot - let it sink in.

Upsound Debra
Govan: So this is like your observation post?

Debra: Yes. We do our observation post. We are listening for the gunshot, voices, any smell.

Govan: Okay.

Voice
Debra Mukansi is one of the 36 women who make up the Black Mambas. Manning hide’s like this one is a key part of night patrol.

Upsound Debra
Govan: What kind of smells do you pick up from here?

Debra: Of cigarettes. And even fires.

Voice
Any sign of intruders will be radioed in to Mamba headquarters.

Upsound Debra
Govan:So what happens when you call it in?

Debra: They will call armed people, so that they will come.

Voice
The Mambas are backed up by armed response teams - ready to respond at a moment’s notice. It’s all coordinated through an operations rooms at Mamba HQ, where each patrol’s location is tracked in real-time.

But being unarmed in the bush means worrying about more than just poachers.

Upsound Debra
Govan: Stop, stop, stop. What is it? That’s a Bush Pig.

Govan: You know you don’t have any guns hey?

Debra: Ja.

Govan: And the lion was here?

Debra: Ja.

Govan: Let’s go.

Debra: And they were walking on the fence line.

Govan: Let’s go.

Debra: (Laughs)

ACT 2


Voice
While the Mambas have been trained to deal with wildlife encounters, is it wise to combat the poaching threat without weapons?

Rather than a fighting force, the women are the eyes and ears of the bush - trained to track and observe poachers and destroy their bush camps.

Upsound Craig Spencer
I don’t believe we should be trying to address this with violence. Because it becomes like a “force continuum”, almost like an arms race.

Voice
Craig Spencer is the founder of the Black Mambas and has spent the past three decades in nature conservation. He believes arming them would escalate the threat from poachers.

Upsound Craig
Because you know what do we do, we take out our old rifles and put on our old camo uniforms and we go and we try and shoot the problem off the landscape again, you know.

Voice
While the battle for the environment continues, unemployment is crippling many communities living alongside our game reserves.

Upsound Goodness Ngobeni
Many of our youth they are not working, they finished school and they did go to tertiary, and they came back with it but they are still not working.

Voice
Like her fellow Mambas, Goodness Ngobeni is from a humble background. She’s from the small village of Makushane just outside Phalaborwa. When she’s not on duty, she spends her time at the home she shares with her mother and daughter.

Upsound Goodness
Govan: I suppose unemployment is everywhere?

Goodness: Yes it is everywhere, but I think in our community it is too much.

Voice
So prevalent in fact that Goodness was willing to risk life and limb to secure a job – even if it meant working with venomous snakes.

Upsound Goodness
Goodness: Because I didn’t know anything about the Black Mambas, I just applied. I thought maybe it was about snakes. So I just applied, and I told myself I am up for a challenge.

Govan: You were preparing yourself to work with snakes?

Goodness: Yes I was ready.

Govan: With Black Mambas?

Goodness: With Black Mambas (laughs)

Voice
Thankfully, they were Mambas in name only.

Upsound Goodness
Govan: When you found out you’d have to walk in the bush, without any weapons, and their were wild animals around, did you have second thoughts? Did you think ah maybe this job’s not for me?

Goodness: I can say that, during our training, I did have second thoughts.

Govan: You did?

Goodness: Yes, because the training it was hard.

Voice
Their efforts have not been in vain. The Mambas have reduced poaching incursions by 62% in the areas they’re deployed in.

Upsound Nkateko
Nakteko: I’m proud working in the bush without guns. Because so many rangers out there in Kruger they’ve been killed because of the guns.

Govan: Right

Nkateko: So when the poachers see them with the guns, they were expecting of fighting.

Voice
Their determination to not back down was demonstrated when Nkateko and her team came across a group of armed meat poachers resting in the bush.

Upsound Nkateko
Nkateko: I end up raising my voice at them and I said: “Hey, don’t stand up, if you stand up I’ll kick you!”

Govan: Laughs

Nkateko: I’m telling you!I was raising my voice like to Hell! They end up going down, they said sorry, sorry! They forgot that they had guns and knives, panga. I thought they were going to harm us. And then I jumped, because we have our handcuffs and pepper spray. And then I took our handcuffs and then we cuffed them.

Govan: You cuffed them?

Nkateko: 100%. And then immediately called the police.

Govan: Ah man, you’re fearless.

Voice
Little wonder she was awarded the prestigious Field Ranger of the Year title in 2023.

Upsound Nkateko.
Nkateko: So once I put on my uniform, and put my boots on the ground, I show them that I can do this. And I can. Don’t say it’s a man’s job.

Govan: And you look good while doing it.

Nkateko: Even us, I can do. Thats why I’m always pushing hard.

Act 3

Link Govan
The Black Mambas are essentially a poaching deterrent - and you may be skeptical but they’ve proven that it works.

Upsound Goodness
So they thought that this job was for men only, so we have proved them wrong, that this job we can do it as women.

Upsound Craig
My personal opinion might be a little bit biased, but they are super effective. And it’s because it’s proactive, it’s not reactive. You know they are knocking on doors, they are writing down who is living in what home, which contractor is working at which lodge, what their vehicle description is, they are visiting everywhere. It’s eyes and ears.

Voice
A uniquely South African iniative that employs, empowers and, crucially, saves lives.

Upsound Nkateko
Nkateko: So us we are not here to fight, we are here to prevent. Just like that.

Govan: But it’s not easy?

Nkateko: It’s not easy, but it’s now been ten years. No one killed by the poacher, no one harmed by the poacher. It’s only us, we’re catching them and taking them out of the reserve. They must not think that we cannot do this, we can. This is a dangerous room, but we can do this.








Promo 1

Voice
Would you take on poachers and wild animals in a game reserve without carrying a gun?

Upsound Debra Mukansi
Govan: Am I the only one that’s nervous?

Debra: Ja! (Laughter)

Govan: Hau, Debra.

Voice
We meet the world’s first ever all female anti poaching unit - and that’s exactly what they’re doing.

Upsound Nkateko
Govan: You cuffed them?

Nkateko: 100%. And then immediately called the police.

Govan: Ah man, you’re fearless.










Promo 2

Upsound Nkateko
Nkateko: I end up raising my voice at them and I said: “Hey, don’t stand up, if you stand up I’ll kick you!”

Voice
How did an unarmed Black Mamba, who’s part of an all female anti poaching unit, become one of the best game rangers in the world?

Voice
We travel to the Greater Kruger, to find out.

Upsound Craig Spencer
I don’t believe we should be trying to address this with violence.





Promo 3
Voice
From humble beginnings to an effective all female Anti Poaching unit…

Upsound Goodness
Govan: You were preparing yourself to work with snakes?

Goodness: Yes I was ready.

Govan: With Black Mambas?

Goodness: With Black Mambas (laughs)

Voice
They’re called the Black Mambas, and they’re taking on the dangers of the South African bush, completely unarmed.

Upsound Nkateko.
Nkateko:I show them that I can do this. And I can.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): They're called the Black Mambas - and they're the world's first all-female anti-poaching unit - we meet some of the women on the front lines of a desperate fight to save our wildlife.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The Black Mambas, named after the well known venomous snake, are 36 young African women who patrol 20 000 hectares of game reserve in the Greater Kruger National Park. Kruger is home to the largest population of Rhino in the world and has also been the vitim of the most poaching attacks. Unlike the gung-ho approach of many anti-poaching units, the Mamba's patrol unarmed, and are spearheading a uniquely South African, innovative approach to wildlife conservation. The Mamba's are focussing their efforts on buy-in from local communities in the area's around Kruger - the same communities where poverty and hardship mean people are easily recruited by poaching syndicates. They also provide eye's and ears on the ground in the areas they patrol. They report, track and trace suspected poaching incursions, destroy bush-meat kitchens and poaching camps, as well as remove remove snares.
metadata.Summary: Their efforts have paid off, they've been incredibly successful in their areas of operation. What's more, they've proven that women can play a valuable role in anti-poaching efforts, a traditionally male dominated field. But who are the women behind the name? In our story we will get to know one or two of the Mamba's, and find out how their own personal struggles have shaped their destinies and lead them into a life on the frontlines of the fight against the international illicit wildlife trade. We'll meet women like Seargeant Leita Nkabela, who grew up in a nearby village. Her family struggled to just put food on the table, and the Kruger Park was seen as a place for the rich, a place they could not visit. But when her brother became a game ranger, Leita's own perceptions on wildlife conservation started to shift. Tragically, her brother was killed in a skirmish with poachers... So why did she decide to get involved?
metadata.Further information: The Black Mambas have had some media exposure, most of it internationally. They are stoked to have Carte Blanche do the story, and have offered us all access.
